title: Special interests
description: Deep-dive starters for the things children love, from dinosaurs and space to horses and gears, building up to real specialisation by 15-17.

nodes.title: Explore
nodes.description: Try simple activities and look at books and pictures.

nodes.title: Investigate
nodes.description: Ask your own questions and test them.

nodes.title: Create
nodes.description: Make something: a model, a chart, a song, a garden.

nodes.title: Share and teach
nodes.description: Explain what you know to someone else.

competencies.title: Keeps an interest journal with 10 entries
Can run a fair test about an interest and record results
Can teach a favourite topic to someone else
Can research a topic independently and write it up
Has developed meaningful depth in one area
Can grow a plant from seed

items.subject: space
items.title: Moon diary
items.summary: The Moon changes shape. Let's draw it!
steps: 🌙 Look at the Moon with a grown-up.
✏️ Draw its shape.
📅 Look again another night.
🌓 Is it bigger? Smaller?
🌕 Find a full, round Moon!

safety.notes: Look from a window, or go outside only with an adult. Never look at the Sun.

basic.description: Draw the Moon from a window.

better.description: Keep a Moon notebook for a month.

advanced.description: Look at Moon craters through binoculars with an adult.

substitutions.use: Your eyes are enough!
Pictures of Moon phases in a book

items.subject: dinosaurs
items.title: Dinosaur footprints
items.summary: Some dinosaurs were huge! How big was a dinosaur foot?
steps: 🦶 Draw round your foot on paper.
🦖 Some big dinosaur footprints were longer than your arm!
📏 Make a big dino footprint from newspaper.
🦕 Stomp like a big dinosaur. Tiptoe like a small one!
❓ Which dinosaur do you like best?

safety.notes: Stomp on a clear, non-slip floor or outside.

better.description: Make a footprint trail across the room.

advanced.description: Draw life-size dinosaur outlines outside with chalk.

substitutions.use: Opened-out cardboard boxes
A stick in sand or soil

items.subject: machines and vehicles
items.title: Vehicle spotter
items.summary: Vehicles help us move. How many can you spot?
steps: 🚗 Car - how many wheels?
🚌 Bus - big or small?
🚲 Bike - 2 wheels!
🚜 Tractor - big wheels!
👀 Look out of the window or at a book.
🖍️ Draw your favourite vehicle.
items.adultNote: Watch from a window or a safe spot well away from the road.

items.subject: oceans
items.title: Into the deep ocean
items.summary: The ocean has layers. The deeper you go, the darker and colder it gets.
steps: Sunlight zone: lots of light. Most sea plants (algae), turtles and many fish live here.
Twilight zone: dim light. Some animals make their own light!
Midnight zone: no sunlight. Animals like anglerfish live here.
The deepest places are trenches, deeper than the tallest mountain is high.
Draw a tall picture of the ocean with each zone and an animal in each.

check.question: Where is there no sunlight?
check.explain: Yes. No sunlight reaches the midnight zone. The only light comes from animals that glow.

items.subject: horses
items.title: How horses see and hear
items.summary: Horses notice the world differently from us. Understanding them helps keep everyone safe.
steps: Horses have eyes on the sides of their heads, so they see almost all the way around.
They have blind spots right behind and just in front of their nose.
Their ears turn towards sounds. Ears pointing back can mean a horse is upset.
Horses are prey animals, so sudden movements and noises can frighten them.
Safety: never walk right behind a horse, and only go near one with an experienced adult.
Draw a horse from above and shade where it cannot see.

check.question: Where should you NOT stand near a horse?
options: Where it can see you, with an adult
check.explain: Right. A horse cannot see directly behind and might kick if startled.

items.subject: gardening
items.title: Sprout a seed in a jar
items.summary: Watch a seed wake up and grow roots and a shoot!
steps: 🫙 Put damp paper inside a clear jar or cup.
🫘 Push a dried bean between the paper and the glass.
💧 Keep the paper damp, not soaking.
👀 Look every day. What comes out first, the root or the shoot?
✏️ Draw it each day.
🪴 When it has leaves, plant it in soil.

hazards: Do not eat raw seeds or beans
safety.notes: Use a plastic cup if possible. Wash hands after. Raw dried beans are not for eating.

basic.description: Sprout one bean and watch it.

better.description: Plant the sprout in soil and keep growing it.

advanced.description: Compare how fast different seeds grow and measure them.

substitutions.use: A clear plastic cup or a cut-down clear plastic bottle (an adult cuts it)
Dried lentils, chickpeas or cress seeds from the kitchen
Any container with a hole in the bottom

items.subject: music
items.title: Water xylophone
items.summary: Different amounts of water make different notes. Make your own instrument!
steps: Line up 5 identical cups or jars.
Pour a different amount of water in each.
Tap each gently with a wooden spoon.
Which has the highest note? The lowest?
Arrange them from low to high.
Play a simple tune you know. Then make up your own!
Science: the sound comes from the cup and water vibrating. More water usually makes a lower note when tapped.

hazards: Glass can crack if hit hard
safety.notes: Tap gently. Use thick jars or sturdy cups, and wipe up spills.

better.description: Colour each note so you can write colour music.

advanced.description: Tune each jar to a real musical scale.

substitutions.use: Sturdy metal cups or bowls
A pencil

items.subject: cooking science
items.title: Shake cream into butter
items.summary: Shake cream long enough and it turns into butter. Why?
steps: Pour cold cream into a jar with a tight lid, half full.
Shake! Take turns.
After a while it becomes whipped cream, then suddenly lumps appear.
The lumps are butter. The liquid is buttermilk.
Science: shaking breaks the tiny fat balls open so the fat sticks together.
Rinse the butter in cold water and taste it on bread.

safety.notes: Check for allergies first. Use a plastic jar if you can. Wash hands before and after. Keep the butter in the fridge.

better.description: Make flavoured butter and compare tastes.

advanced.description: Test which cream turns to butter faster and why.

substitutions.use: A clean plastic bottle with a cap
Watch a video of the process if cream is too costly

items.subject: sport science
items.title: Heartbeat science
items.summary: Measure how exercise changes your heart rate, like a sport scientist.
steps: Sit still for 2 minutes. Find your pulse on your wrist or neck.
Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. That is beats per minute.
Do 1 minute of star jumps or jogging on the spot.
Measure again straight away, then every minute until it returns to normal.
Draw a line graph of your results.
Think: why does your heart speed up? What does recovery time tell you?

safety.notes: Exercise at a comfortable level on a non-slip surface. Stop if you feel dizzy, sick or in pain, and tell an adult. Children with heart or breathing conditions should follow their doctor's advice.

materials: A clock with a second hand or a timer
basic.description: Measure and graph your own heart rate.

better.description: Compare results across family members and different exercises.

materials: Fitness watch or phone heart-rate app
advanced.description: Compare your hand count with a device. Which is more accurate?

substitutions.use: Count "one-and-two-and" or use a phone clock
Jogging on the spot indoors

items.subject: building and architecture
items.title: Strongest paper bridge
items.summary: Engineers use shapes to make bridges strong. How strong can you make a paper bridge?
steps: Put two piles of books 20 cm apart.
Lay a flat sheet of paper across. Add coins. How many before it falls?
Now fold the paper: try a zigzag, a tube or a U-shape.
Test each with coins and record results.
Which shape is strongest? Why?
Look for these shapes in real bridges and buildings.

safety.notes: Keep coins away from toddlers. Handle paper edges carefully.

better.description: Build a truss bridge from straws.

advanced.description: Build a stick bridge and test it with a bag of rice.

substitutions.use: Small stones, dried beans or washers
Two boxes or chairs

items.subject: art history
items.title: Art through time and around the world
items.summary: People have made art for tens of thousands of years, everywhere on Earth. Make an art timeline!
steps: Cave paintings: some of the oldest known paintings are tens of thousands of years old.
Ancient Egypt: wall paintings and sculptures for tombs and temples.
Chinese ink painting: mountains and water painted with brushes on silk or paper.
Islamic art: beautiful geometric patterns and calligraphy.
European Renaissance: painters studied perspective and the human body.
Indian miniature painting, Japanese woodblock prints, West African sculpture, and modern art too.
Make a timeline on a long strip of paper. Draw your own small copy of one artwork in its style.
items.adultNote: Free museum websites and library books have high-quality images. Talk about where art comes from and who made it.

items.subject: coding games
items.title: Design your own game
items.summary: Game designers test ideas on paper before coding. Design a game, test it, then code it if you can.
steps: Choose a goal: what does the player try to do?
Write the rules: turns, moves, how you win.
Make a paper prototype: a board, cards or a sketch of each screen.
Play-test with family. Write down what is confusing or boring.
Change one rule at a time and test again.
Optional: code a simple version with block or text coding.
Teach someone new to play it.

safety.notes: Take breaks from screens. Paper versions need no screen at all.

better.description: Make a polished board or card game.

advanced.cost: Free with a computer or phone
advanced.description: Turn your design into a simple digital game.

substitutions.use: A paper prototype is a real game designer's tool
Numbered paper slips in a cup

items.subject: space
items.title: Find the constellations
items.summary: Stars form patterns called constellations. People in different cultures saw different pictures in the same stars.
steps: Find a dark spot with an adult, away from bright lights.
Wait 15 minutes for your eyes to adjust.
Use a star chart (printed or on a phone with the screen dimmed) to find one easy constellation.
Sketch it and note the date and time.
Research what different cultures called that star pattern.
Look again in a month. Has it moved? Why?

safety.notes: Adult supervision required outside at night: the adult chooses a safe spot away from roads and water and stays with you. Dress warmly and use a torch to walk. Never look at the Sun, with or without binoculars.

materials: A free star chart from a library
Torch covered with red paper or cellophane
better.description: Use red light to read charts without spoiling night vision.

advanced.description: Look for star clusters and the moons of Jupiter.

substitutions.use: A dimmed phone with a free star-map app
Draw constellations from a book indoors

sources.title: Accident prevention advice
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)

items.subject: dinosaurs
items.title: Be a fossil detective
items.summary: Fossils form over millions of years. Make a model fossil and learn how real ones are found and studied.
steps: Learn: most fossils form when a living thing is buried quickly in mud or sand, which slowly turns to rock.
Press a shell, leaf or toy dinosaur into salt dough or clay to make an imprint ("trace fossil").
Let it air-dry for a day or two.
Bury the fossils in a tray of sand. Ask someone to dig them out carefully with a brush, like a palaeontologist.
Record each find: draw it, measure it, guess what made it.
Research one real fossil find and how scientists worked out its age.

hazards: Plaster gets warm as it sets
safety.notes: An adult supervises. Wash hands after and do not eat the dough. Dig gently. Plaster of Paris (advanced version only) is mixed and poured by the adult; it gets hot as it sets and can burn badly, so never put hands or any body part into setting plaster.

advanced.description: With an adult, make plaster cast fossils.

substitutions.use: Salt dough (2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, about 1 cup water)
A box of soil outside
Salt dough

sources.title: Accident prevention advice
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)

items.subject: machines and vehicles
items.title: How gears work
items.summary: Gears trade speed for strength. Count the teeth to work out a gear ratio.
steps: Look at a bicycle (with an adult) and find the front and back gears (sprockets).
Count the teeth on the front gear you are using and the back gear.
Gear ratio = front teeth ÷ back teeth. A bigger number means more speed, harder pedalling.
Turn the pedal one full turn slowly and count how many times the back wheel turns.
Does it match your ratio?
Find other gears: in a hand whisk, a clock or a toy.

hazards: Fingers caught in chain or spokes
safety.notes: Keep fingers away from the chain and wheel while turning. Have an adult hold the bike steady or turn it upside down safely. Wash hands after.

basic.description: Count teeth and calculate the ratio.

better.description: Make cardboard gears and test ratios.

advanced.description: Build gear trains and measure speed and force.

substitutions.use: A hand whisk, egg beater or drawings of gears
Bottle-top gears with card teeth

items.subject: horses
items.title: Equine science
items.summary: Go deeper into horses: anatomy, digestion, welfare and the careers that care for them.
steps: Anatomy: horses walk on a single toe, the hoof. Hooves grow and need regular care from a farrier.
Digestion: horses evolved to graze for many hours a day on grasses and hay.
Welfare: good care means the right food and water, shelter, exercise, company of other horses and vet care.
Behaviour: horses are herd animals and communicate with body language, such as ear and tail position.
Careers: equine vet, farrier, stable manager, equine physiotherapist, researcher.
Research one topic in depth and make a one-page fact sheet.
Any hands-on time with horses should be with a qualified, experienced adult.
items.adultNote: Riding and handling are covered by qualified instructors, not this lesson.

items.subject: gardening
items.title: A real growing experiment
items.summary: Design a fair test with plants and analyse the results like a scientist.
steps: Ask a question, such as "Does more light make beans grow taller?"
Choose one thing to change (the variable) and keep everything else the same.
Grow at least 3 plants per group so results are fair.
Measure every few days for 3-4 weeks and record in a table.
Draw a graph and work out the average for each group.
Write a short report: question, method, results, conclusion and what you would improve.

hazards: Some plants and seeds are poisonous
safety.notes: Wear gloves or wash hands after handling soil. Use common food-crop seeds and do not eat seeds or experimental plants.

basic.description: Grow plants in containers on a windowsill.

better.description: Run a careful test with 3 groups.

advanced.description: Test soil type or fertiliser and compare with a soil test.

substitutions.use: Containers on a windowsill or balcony
Yogurt pots or cut plastic bottles with holes
A strip of paper marked with a ruler at a library

items.subject: sport science
items.title: Design a safe training plan
items.summary: Use sport science to plan four weeks of training for a goal you choose.
steps: Pick a goal: run 2 km without stopping, improve flexibility, or learn a skill.
Measure your starting point safely.
Plan: warm-up, main activity, cool-down. Increase difficulty gradually, a little each week.
Include rest days: muscles get stronger while recovering.
Think about sleep, water and food.
Keep a training log and measure again after 4 weeks.
Write what worked and what you would change.

safety.notes: Build up gradually, warm up and cool down, drink water and stop if anything hurts. Anyone with a health condition or injury should check with a doctor first. Avoid heavy weights without qualified coaching.

basic.description: Bodyweight exercises or running, logged on paper.

advanced.description: Track data and get feedback from a qualified coach.

substitutions.use: Bodyweight exercises at home or a park
A measured route with an adult's approval

items.subject: specialisation
items.title: Choose your specialisation
items.summary: Pick one area to explore in real depth over several months. Become someone who truly knows and can do something.
steps: Look back at your interest journal and passport: what keeps pulling you back?
Choose one area. It can change later - depth in anything teaches you how to go deep.
Set a big question or goal, for example "Grow 20 kinds of vegetables", "Build a working robot" or "Understand how black holes form".
Make a learning plan: books, courses, projects, and people (an adult helps find mentors).
Spend a few hours every week for at least 3 months. Keep a log.
Create something real: a portfolio, a report, a model, a performance.
Contribute: teach a younger child, give a talk, or help a community group with your skills.

safety.notes: Check the safety rating of every practical activity in your plan. Anything amber or red needs the right supervision.

basic.description: Self-directed study and projects with free resources.

better.description: Add a real build, garden, performance or experiment.

advanced.description: Work with a mentor or take a recognised course.

substitutions.use: Letters or calls with a family friend who works in the field, or recorded public lectures
Basic version of the project with household materials

items.adultNote: This is the brief's "at least one area of meaningful depth". Let the young person choose; support with time, materials and introductions.

items.subject: specialisation
items.title: Write a research report
items.summary: Research a question in your interest area and write a report others can learn from.
steps: Write a clear, focused question.
Find at least 5 sources: books, reputable websites, interviews or your own data.
Check each source: who wrote it, when, and what evidence do they use?
Take notes in your own words, and record where each idea came from.
Write: introduction, what you found, discussion, conclusion and references.
Ask someone to review it, then improve it.
Share it: present it to family or a group.

better.description: Use free reputable online sources and type notes.

advanced.description: Produce a formatted report with charts and references.

substitutions.use: A public library
Read it aloud or handwrite a neat copy
